claims.text: Effective communication occurs when the intended message reaches the intended receiver and is understood as intended. Sending a message is not sufficient evidence that this happened. Business communication coordinates work, explains objectives, supports decisions and maintains relationships with staff, customers and suppliers. An accurate production instruction can still fail if it arrives after the work is completed or uses language the receiver does not understand. Feedback helps test understanding, especially where the message requires action. Communication should therefore fit the audience, purpose, urgency and need for a record. Effectiveness does not require the receiver to agree with every proposal: a worker can understand an unwelcome change clearly and still object. Managers should distinguish disagreement from misunderstanding and allow appropriate questions.

claims.text: Internal communication takes place within the business; external communication crosses its boundary to customers, suppliers or other outside parties. One-way communication sends information without a response as part of that exchange; two-way communication includes feedback between sender and receiver. These distinctions describe different features and can be combined. An internal staff discussion is internal and two-way; a supplier conversation is external and two-way; a notice to staff can be internal and one-way. Written does not automatically mean one-way, since an email exchange can include replies, and speaking is not automatically two-way if no response is allowed. Identify the parties and the opportunity for feedback instead of assuming the medium settles every classification.

claims.text: Verbal communication uses spoken words, written communication uses text and visual communication uses images, symbols or graphical displays. Letters and meetings are methods, while these ways describe how meaning is expressed. A meeting can combine spoken discussion, written handouts and a visual diagram. Verbal discussion can give fast clarification and personal contact, but may leave no reliable record unless recorded appropriately. Written text provides something to consult and can specify details, but the receiver must access and understand it; replies may not be immediate. Visuals can make a layout or trend clearer, but unfamiliar symbols or missing labels can mislead. Choose using urgency, audience access and language, complexity, confidentiality, cost and the need for feedback or proof. Combining methods can be more suitable than claiming one is best for every message.

claims.text: The sender originates the message, the message is the information intended, the medium is the channel used, timing concerns when it is sent and received, the receiver is the intended recipient, and feedback is a response indicating receipt or understanding. The elements must work together. A correct message sent through an inaccessible channel fails to reach its receiver. A clear instruction received too late cannot guide the intended action. Feedback can reveal a misunderstanding so the sender can clarify it; merely observing that a system delivered a notification does not prove comprehension. Good communication checks who needs to know, what they need to understand, how to reach them and by when. Use plain wording and relevant detail rather than overload the receiver with unrelated information.

claims.text: Communication barriers include noise, unfamiliar language or jargon, ambiguous wording, inaccessible channels, poor timing, information overload, long reporting chains and attitudes that discourage listening or honest feedback. Match the remedy to the cause. Move a safety briefing away from loud machinery; use plain language and check meaning where terms are unfamiliar; give dates and responsibilities instead of vague instructions; use a channel the receiver can access. Send information early enough to act and prioritise the essential message instead of burying it in many notices. Shorter communication routes can reduce distortion, while respectful opportunities for questions can reveal hidden misunderstanding. Repeating the same unclear message more loudly does not necessarily solve a language problem. A method is effective in its circumstances, not because it is modern or widely used.
